title: At the doctor's
goal: Say which part of your body hurts, and use pronouns in the Akkusativ and Dativ — *mich*, *mir*, *dich*, *dir*.
bekal: name parts of the body and symptoms
use *wehtun* and other verbs that take the Dativ
understand the doctor's advice and how to take medicine

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ich fühle mich nicht gut
dialogs.intro: Budi has had a fever for two days and finally goes to the doctor's office. Watch the little pronouns in each sentence — *mir*, *mich*, *Ihnen* — and which form appears where.

lines.speaker: Ärztin:
lines.text: Guten Tag, Herr Santoso. Was fehlt Ihnen?
lines.id: Hello, Mr. Santoso. What seems to be the problem?
lines.literal: good day, Mr. Santoso. what lacks to-you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich fühle mich seit zwei Tagen nicht gut.
lines.id: I haven't been feeling well for two days.
lines.literal: I feel myself since two days not good.

lines.speaker: Ärztin:
lines.id: Are you in pain? Where exactly?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mein Kopf tut weh. Und der Hals auch.
lines.id: My head hurts. And my throat too.
lines.literal: my head does pain. and the throat too.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, gestern hatte ich achtunddreißig Grad.
lines.id: Yes, yesterday I had thirty-eight degrees.
lines.literal: yes, yesterday had I eight-and-thirty degree.

lines.speaker: Ärztin:
lines.text: Machen Sie bitte den Mund auf. Sagen Sie „Ah".
lines.literal: make you please the mouth open. say you "Ah".

lines.speaker: Ärztin:
lines.text: Das ist eine Erkältung. Nichts Schlimmes. Ich gebe Ihnen ein Rezept.
lines.id: It's a cold. Nothing serious. I'll give you a prescription.
lines.literal: that is a cold. nothing bad. I give to-you a prescription.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Do I have to stay at home?

lines.speaker: Ärztin:
lines.text: Ja, drei Tage. Sie sollen viel trinken und viel schlafen.
lines.id: Yes, three days. You should drink a lot and sleep a lot.
lines.literal: yes, three days. you should much drink and much sleep.

lines.speaker: Ärztin:
lines.text: Dreimal täglich nach dem Essen. Gute Besserung!
lines.id: Three times a day after meals. Get well soon!
lines.literal: three-times daily after the meal. good recovery!

notes: ***Was fehlt Ihnen?*** literally "what are you lacking?", meaning "what seems to be the problem?". It's the standard opening line of every doctor's visit in Germany. The standard beginner's reply: *Ich fühle mich nicht gut.*

***sich fühlen*** needs a pronoun pointing back to the subject: *ich fühle **mich***, *du fühlst **dich***, *er fühlt **sich*** — a bit like English "myself", "yourself". German has many verbs like this (*sich freuen*, *sich setzen*), and they're covered fully in A2; for now, learn *ich fühle mich* as a whole.

***wehtun* takes the Dativ.** You can say *Mir tut der Kopf weh* or *Mein Kopf tut weh* — both are correct and equally common. If more than one thing hurts, the verb goes plural: *Mir tun die Füße weh.*

***Ich gebe Ihnen ein Rezept*** has two objects at once: the **receiver** in the Dativ (*Ihnen*) and the **thing** in the Akkusativ (*ein Rezept*) — English does the same in "I'll give **you** **a prescription**". This is the second use of the Dativ, after places in unit 13 — and it will grow fully in A2.
***sollen* for a doctor's advice.** *Sie sollen viel trinken* = "you should drink a lot", an instruction coming from someone else. Compare *Sie müssen*, which is an absolute must.
**Line 7: *Machen Sie den Mund auf*.** *Aufmachen* (to open) is a separable verb, so the prefix still flies to the end even when the sentence is a command.

grammars.title: Pronouns in three forms
body: Personal pronouns change form according to their role in the sentence, just like articles. English does this too, a little — *I → me*, *he → him* — but German has one more form, so this table is worth learning whole.
after: Notice that *wir*, *ihr* and *Sie* use **the same form** in the Akkusativ and Dativ (*uns*, *euch*, *Sie/Ihnen* — the first two are truly identical). The only ones you really need to tell apart are at the top: *mich/mir*, *dich/dir*, *ihn/ihm*.

When to use which? **Akkusativ** when it's the direct object of the action: *Ich sehe **dich***, *Er ruft **mich** an*. **Dativ** when it's the receiver or the one affected: *Er hilft **mir***, *Ich gebe **dir** das Buch*, *Wie geht es **dir**?*
⚠️ *Ihnen* with a capital letter means "to you" (formal); *ihnen* in lowercase means "to them". Once again, the capital letter saves the day.

grammars.title: Verbs that take the Dativ
body: A small group of verbs takes the Dativ, not the Akkusativ, even though in English they feel like they have an ordinary object. There are only a few — learn them as a list.
after: *Gefallen* hides a small trap: the subject isn't the person but the **thing**. *Berlin gefällt mir* is literally "Berlin pleases me". That's why the verb follows the thing: *Die Bücher gefall**en** mir.*
The last row, *geben*, uses **both** at once: the receiver in the Dativ, the thing in the Akkusativ. The same pattern works for *schicken* (send), *zeigen* (show) and *bringen* (bring).

head: German
English
rows: I have a cough and a runny nose.

blocks.text: Notice the *-schmerzen* pattern: body part + *Schmerzen* gives you the name of the complaint — just like English "head**ache**", "stomach**ache**". *Kopf* → *Kopfschmerzen*, *Bauch* → *Bauchschmerzen*, *Zahn* → *Zahnschmerzen*, *Rücken* → *Rückenschmerzen*. One pattern, every complaint.

sections.title: At the pharmacy and the doctor's office

head: German
English
rows: Do you have something for a headache?
Wie oft muss ich das nehmen?
How often do I have to take this?
Three times a day after meals.

blocks.text: ⚠️ In Germany, any medicine stronger than a mild painkiller is only sold at the **Apotheke**, often with a prescription — not at the supermarket or the *Drogerie*. And if you're sick for more than three days, your employer will ask for a ***Krankschreibung***, a doctor's sick note.

blocks.title: Emergency numbers
items: **112** — ambulance and fire service, valid all over Europe, free from any phone.
**116 117** — out-of-hours doctor service (*ärztlicher Bereitschaftsdienst*), for problems that aren't emergencies.
Sentences to remember: *Ich brauche einen Arzt* and *Bitte rufen Sie einen Krankenwagen.*
Ich gebe ____ das Rezept. (to you, formal)

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: What seems to be the problem? — I don't feel well. — My head hurts. — Do you have a fever? — You should drink a lot. — Three times a day after meals.
